The Crawford Project site is located within the stable craton of the North American plate, in Northern Ontario region, characterized by a recently deglaciated shield terrain with numerous lakes, crystalline bedrock exposures, and variable glacial till deposits (Chapter 0). While Northern Ontario has a low rate of seismicity, notable intraplate seismicity has been recorded, driven primarily by Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) and regional intraplate stress. These forces, along with the reactivation of crustal faults and fractures, contribute to the region's earthquake activity.

fields.text: The seismicity analysis for the Crawford Project site (Chapter 0) is based on data from publicly available databases, which were utilized to update the seismic catalog within a 400-kilometer radius of the site. The updated and declustered catalog documents 67 events with moment magnitudes (Mw) of 3 or greater, spanning from 1916 to August 30, 2026. Historical events such as the 1935 Temiskamingue earthquake (Mw 6.2) and the 2000 Kipawa earthquake (Mw 4.7) demonstrate the potential for notable seismic activity.

The seismic hazard assessment for the Crawford Project site (Chapter 0) utilized the 6th Generation Seismic Hazard Model of Canada (CanadaSHM6) (Canadian Comission on Building and Fires Codes and National Research Council of Canada, 2020), as implemented in the Global Earthquake Model (GEM) (2018). This model, which was used as the basis for the seismic hazard values in the 2020 National Building Code of Canada (2020 NBCC), consists of three regional models: the Western Model, the East Arctic Model, and the Southeastern Model. The Crawford Project site falls within the Southeastern Model.

The ground motion intensity for the Crawford Project site (Chapter 0) in Southeastern Canada is modeled using two sets of Ground Motion Models (GMMs) within the CanadaSHM6 framework. Each set is assigned an equal probability of 0.5. The first set, developed by Atkinson and Adams (2013)(AA13), includes three models, named "upper," "central," and "lower", to capture epistemic uncertainty. The central model, which represents the median ground motion, carries the highest weight. The second set of GMMs is derived from the Central and Eastern North America project (NGA-East-13) (Goulet, et al., 2017) and includes 13 candidate models, with weights that vary depending on the natural vibration period.

The PSHA for the Site was conducted using the OpenQuake v3.26.2 engine. Results of the PSHA are presented in terms of Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) and Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS) for site conditions ranging from hard to soft rock, as defined by the 2020 NBCC (Chapter 6). The analysis considers events associated with a target AEP of 1:475, 1: 975, 1:2,475, 1:5,000 and 1:10,000 years and for various confidence levels, including mean, 50th, 84th, 90th, and 95th percentiles.

fields.text: The PSHA for the Site was conducted using the OpenQuake v3.26.2 engine. Results of the PSHA are presented in terms of Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) and Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS) for site conditions ranging from hard to soft rock, as defined by the 2020 NBCC (Chapter 6). The analysis considers events associated with a target AEP of 1:475, 1: 975, 1:2,475, 1:5,000 and 1:10,000 years and for various confidence levels, including mean, 50th, 84th, 90th, and 95th percentiles.

Dynamic site response analysis was used to modify the response spectra to the specific geotechnical conditions of each project facility (Chapter 6.5). This analysis involves estimating multi-period amplification factors dependent on the average shear-wave velocity of the upper 30 m of soil (Vs,30) as defined by the 2020 NBCC. The design demands combine the direct logic-tree evaluation at each condition with the ST20 transformation of the demand at the reference condition of 760 m/s, conditioned on the PGA of the same realization. Seismic Cone Penetration Tests (SCPT) conducted during the 2021-2022 and 2023 field investigations (SRK Consulting (Canada), Inc., 2023) (2024) provided Vs,30 values ranging from 180 to 230 m/s. A characteristic Vs,30value of 220 m/s was adopted for the site, classifying it as Stiff Soil Class D per the 2020 NBCC. The resulting UHS for these site-specific conditions were presented for target AEPs of ranging from 1:475 to 1:10,000 years and for various confidence levels.

The 2020 NBCC offers an online seismic hazard tool that provides seismic hazard values for building design across Canada (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021d). A comparison of the mean response spectra from this tool with the PSHA analysis was conducted, covering the relevant AEPs and structural periods (Chapter 8). The ratios of the PSHA spectral ordinates to the NRC 2020 values range from 0.70 to 1.30 for the periods and site conditions compared.

The Canadian Dam Association (CDA) (2013) along with the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) (2020) and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) (2011), recommends performing PSHA and determining recurrence intervals based on the potential consequences of dam failure, which range from “Low” to “Extreme.” For this project, an “Extreme” consequence level has been designated for the FEED phase of the TMF, leading to a designation of the “Maximum Design Earthquake” (MDE) with an AEP of 1:10,000 years, consistent with GISTM and, for closure, with ICOLD and ANCOLD guidance. For the Clay, Rock, and Sand & Silt Impoundments, as well as the East and West Stockpiles, the MDE corresponds to an AEP of 1: 2,475 years. Response spectra and PGA values for the MDE have been provided for various site conditions, from hard rock to stiff soil, and at different confidence levels (Chapter 0). For stiff soils (Vs,30= 220 m/s), the MDE for the TMF is anticipated to result in a horizontal Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) of 0.312 g (mean) and 0.442 g (84th percentile) and the MDE for the impoundments and stockpiles is anticipated to result in a PGA of 0.159 g (mean) and 0.229 g (84th percentile).

Chapter 1 corresponds to the introduction to the project, background, objectives, and scope.

target.text: Introduction

fields.text: Chapter 2  describes the seismotectonics framework of the area to provide an understanding of the sources that may be seismically active.

target.text: Seismotectonics

fields.text: Chapter 3 presents a brief description of the seismicity study area (defined within 400-km radius of the Site), which includes the development of a regional seismicity catalog compiled and updated to include events up to August 30, 2026 and a brief description of the most significant historic earthquakes in the seismicity study area.

target.text: Seismicity

fields.text: Chapter 3 presents a brief description of the seismicity study area (defined within 400-km radius of the Site), which includes the development of a regional seismicity catalog compiled and updated to include events up to August 30, 2026 and a brief description of the most significant historic earthquakes in the seismicity study area.
Chapter 4 describes the source model and characterizes sources capable of producing significant ground-motion at the Site to be used in the probabilistic hazard assessment.

target.text: Seismic Source Model

fields.text: Chapter 5 presents the ground motion models selected to be used in the seismic hazard analysis to estimate the strong ground motion that may occur at the Site if an earthquake of a certain magnitude occurs at a nearby location.

target.text: Ground Motion Intensity Model

fields.text: Chapter 6 presents the development of seismic hazard analysis in rock including hazard deaggregation, to identify contributing events for a given ground motion intensity and annual exceedance probability (AEP) or return period.

target.text: Seismic Hazard

fields.text: Chapter 7 presents the site response to determine ground motions at the surface level. Chapter 6.5 also includes the characterization of the site foundation in terms of the average shear wave velocity to a depth of 30 m (Vs,30) using information from the past field geotechnical and geophysical investigations of 2021-2022 and 2023.

target.text: Site Response

fields.text: Chapter 7 presents the site response to determine ground motions at the surface level. Chapter 6.5 also includes the characterization of the site foundation in terms of the average shear wave velocity to a depth of 30 m (Vs,30) using information from the past field geotechnical and geophysical investigations of 2021-2022 and 2023.

target.text: Controlling Scenarios

fields.text: Chapter 8 provides a comparison of the seismic hazard estimates developed for this study with the 2020 National Building Code of Canada.

target.text: 2020 National Building Code of Canada Seismic Hazard Values

fields.text: Chapter 9 summarizes design events for this study selected for a target AEP.

target.text: Design Earthquakes

fields.text: Chapter 10 provides estimates of slope design parameters, including seismic (pseudo-static) coefficients (kh) using empirical correlations. Values of kh are presented for the selected design event and for a range of target displacements (𝑑𝑎) for various embankment materials (in terms of shear wave velocities) and embankment geometries.

target.text: Slope Design Parameters

fields.text: Chapter 11 provides conclusions of the present study.

target.text: Conclusions

While majority of this area appears to be predominantly of low seismicity, it contains several zones of concentrated seismic activity, particularly along the eastern continental margin and in specific clusters within the craton. The Natural Resources of Canada (NRC) (2021a) has grouped these seismic clusters in seven regions, as shown in Figure 21.

Notable intraplate seismicity has been observed, as depicted in Figure 22 (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021a) and Figure 23 (Ma, Eaton, & Adams, 2008). The causes of earthquakes in this region have been primarily linked to:

Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA): ongoing process of the Earth's crust to rebound from the weight of the last ice sheets tat has been associated with seismicity in Northern Ontario (Ma, Eaton, & Adams, 2008) (Mazzotti, 2005) (Wu & Hasegawa, 1996), and crustal faults and fractures (Adams & Basham, 1991).

Regional intraplate stress: intraplate stress caused by ongoing deformation of the plate, including residual effects of ancient tectonic processes and current tectonic forces that can induce earthquakes (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021a; Adams & Basham, 1991).
Crustal faults and fractures: Existing weaknesses in the crust can be reactivated by the stresses associated with GIA and intraplate tectonic forces, leading to seismic events (Adams & Basham, 1991).

The combined, updated, and declustered catalog contains  67 events within the study area with moment magnitudes (Mw) ≥ 3, as shown in Figure 31 of which 67 have Mw ≥ 3, and listed in Table A1. These events span the period from 1916 to August 30, 2026. Declustering to remove dependent aftershocks and foreshocks followed the Gardner and Knopoff (1974) statistical method. It was applied to the combined multi-source catalog before selecting the Mw ≥ 3 subset. Records of one source catalog within 10 s and 100 km of a larger or equal event of that catalog were also removed before declustering, because they are alternative solutions of a single earthquake. The updated catalog was used solely to illustrate the most current seismicity in the project site region and was not used to update to recurrence in the 2020 National Building Code of Canada (2020 NBCC) (Canadian Comission on Building and Fires Codes and National Research Council of Canada, 2020).

On November 1, 1935, at 1:03 am local time, an earthquake occurred about 10 km east of Témiscaming, Québec, approximately 285 km southeast of the Site. The earthquake was felt as far west as Thunder Bay, Ontario (later known as Fort William), as far east as the Bay of Fundy, and as far south as Kentucky and Virginia (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021d).

In Témiscaming, Québec, around 80% of chimneys were damaged, indicating a Modified Mercalli intensity of VII. Cracks also appeared in brick walls, and minor rockfalls were observed in the epicentral area. The shake caused significant damage in nearby Mattawa and North Bay, where many chimneys were destroyed. Numerous aftershocks were felt in Témiscaming and Kipawa in the months that followed. The day after the earthquake, Tee Lake's water near the epicenter was discolored, likely due to the resuspension of gyttja (freshwater mud). Additionally, 300 km away near Parent, Québec, the earthquake triggered a 30-meter railroad embankment slide (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021d).

On January 1, 2000, an Mw 4.7 earthquake occurred beneath Lac Kipawa, about 10 km north of the town of Témiscaming, Quebec, and approximately 286 km southeast of the Site. The earthquake was felt over distances exceeding 500 km. Residents within 50 km of the epicenter reported intense shaking (intensity MM VI), which caused minor damage, including fallen light objects, a broken ventilation pipe, and cracks in plaster. The earthquake was felt in Témiscaming, North Bay, and as far away as Toronto, making it one of Canada's most significant earthquakes in 2000 (Natural Resources de Canada, 2013).

The first set of GMMs was provided by Atkinson and Adams (2013) hereafter referred to as AA13. This set was developed for eastern stable crustal earthquakes and included three GMMs to account for epistemic uncertainty. These three models were termed “upper,” “central,” and “lower” GMMs, with associated weights of 0.25, 0.50, and 0.25, respectively. The central GMM in AA13 is constructed by taking the arithmetic average of five candidate GMMs. The upper and lower GMM curves are obtained by adding and subtracting the standard deviation (in the logarithmic scale), each with a weight of 0.25. The central GMM represents the median curve with a weight of 0.50.

The second set, based on the Central and Eastern North America project (NGA-East-13), was provided by Goulet et al (2017). The NGA-East-13 is obtained by weighting a set of 13 candidate GMMs using weights that depend on the natural vibration period (Tn). The standard deviation for NGA-East-13 is the same as that for AA13.

A PSHA for the Site was conducted using the CanadaSHM6 hazard model (Natural Resources of Canada, 2020) as implemented in the OpenQuake engine v.3.26.2 (Pagani, Monelli, & Weatgerill, 2014). The AEP curves present the direct logic-tree calculation. The tabulated design values and UHS combine this evaluation with the ST20 transformation of the demand at the reference condition of 760 m/s, conditioned on the PGA of the same realization. The results are presented in terms of AEP and UHS for various site conditions as defined by the 2020 NBCC (Canadian Comission on Building and Fires Codes and National Research Council of Canada, 2020). Site classification, described in Section 7.1, are based on a shear wave velocity profile measured from the ground surface to a depth of 30 meters (Vs,30).

Site classification, described in Section 7.1, are based on a shear wave velocity profile measured from the ground surface to a depth of 30 meters (Vs,30).

Site amplification factors from GMMs of the CanadaSHM6 were adopted in the direct calculation. The design demands combine the direct logic-tree evaluation at each condition with the ST20 transformation of the demand at the reference condition of 760 m/s, conditioned on the PGA of the same realization. These GMMs use the following amplification factors (Kolaj, Allen, Mayfied, Adams, & Halchuk, 2019):

The AA13 GMMs (Atkinson & Adams, Ground motion prediction equations for application to the 2015 Canadian national seismic hazard maps, 2013) employ of amplification factors from the 2015 National Building Code of Canada (2015 NBCC) (Canadian Commission on Building and Fire Codes and National Research Council of Canada, 2015). For sites with Vs,30 ≤ 760 m/s, these amplification factors F(T) were derived from the active crust GMM of Boore & Atkinson (BA08) (2008). For sites with Vs,30> 760 m/s, the factors are based on a conversion from 2000 to 760 m/s using the AA13 model, which is derived from the stable crust GMM by Atkinson and Boore (2006). These amplification factors vary the spectral period and the probabilistic PGA hazard for Site Class C, allowing the adjustment of the hazard spectra to match the specific Site Class.

The dam classification for the TMF, reviewed during the feasibility study (WSP, 2023) (Ausenco, 2023), indicated a “Very High” consequence during construction, operation, and transition and closure active care phases, and “Significant” during the closure passive care phase. For this study, an “Extreme” consequence level has been designated for the FEED phase of the project TMF embankments as defined by CDA (2013). PSHA: The PSHA for the site was conducted using the OpenQuake v3.26.2 engine (Pagani, Monelli, & Weatgerill, 2014). Results are presented in terms of Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) and Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS) for site conditions ranging from hard to soft rock, as defined by the 2020 NBCC. The analysis considers events with target AEPs of 1:475, 1:975, 1:2,475, 1:5,000, and 1:10,000 years, and covers various confidence levels, including mean, 50th, 84th, 90th, and 95th percentiles.
